newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam assembly to meet amid uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam assembly to meet amid uncertainty.

text.p: Vietnam's National Assembly is due to convene next week for its autumn session facing a range of still-unresolved questions from a landmark Communist Party meeting held earlier this year.
The month-long meeting will see final endorsement of a five-year policy plan approved at the congress, as well as changes to foreign investment rules, and a new law on legal documents.

But at a rare joint news briefing on Friday for foreign and domestic journalists there was little sign that continued uncertainty over Vietnam's 10-year-old reform process would be resolved by the coming session.
National Assembly spokesman Vu Mao and other government officials fielded instead questions over problems from corruption to poverty to economic woes to journalists' rights.
Mao said new tax laws would be discussed but not completed during the session. He gave no details but indicated government personnel changes would also be announced.
"You could say they were making an effort to try today," said a foreign diplomat who attended the briefing. "But I was expecting more happening in this session than approval of just two laws."

Vietnam's Communist Party congress drew to a close in early July after affirming the need to maintain the leading role of socialism in a country still undergoing the sometimes painful process of a shift to a market economy.
But political analysts say the tone of the conclave, normally held once every five years, was less positive than on previous occasions.
Partly as a result a previously anticipated post-congress rebound in economic sentiment -- particularly among members of the $22 billion foreign investment community -- has yet to materialise.
"Compared with a year ago the feeling is we're not seeing the same impetus behind the reforms," a Hanoi-based diplomat said at the end of Friday's briefing.
Mao did not refer directly to the concerns but said revisions to the foreign investment law would create a more open, convenient and diversified environment for overseas business.
He said investment would be promoted in the production of goods for export and in the agricultural commodities sector.
A 25-page press statement issued at Friday's meeting said lawmakers would be told the country's socio-economic situation had seen continued positive changes in the first nine months of the year.

It said Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth would reach 9.5 percent, industrial production 14 percent and inflation would stay below seven percent, while rice output would exceed a 28 million tonne target by 200,000 tonnes.
